about.title: Lynwood Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A fall rarely feels like a legal matter in the moment. You are on the ground outside a market on Long Beach Boulevard, or in a stairwell at an apartment complex off Imperial Highway, and the only thought is whether you can stand back up. Later, when the bills start arriving, the question changes: who was responsible for the spill nobody cleaned, the cracked step nobody repaired, the parking-lot hole nobody marked? Under California law, the answer turns on notice. An owner or tenant in Lynwood is generally responsible when they knew about a hazard, or reasonably should have known, and did not fix it or warn people. Proving that depends on evidence that disappears fast: surveillance footage gets overwritten, a puddle gets mopped, a witness walks off. LawProactive is a free connection service, not a law firm. We match people hurt on someone else's property in Lynwood and nearby parts of Los Angeles County with an independent attorney who takes premises cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Lynwood Residents Use LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice is the heart of the case
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can pursue inspection logs, prior complaints, and maintenance records that speak to how long the problem sat there.

items.title: Video and photos vanish quickly
items.desc: Many Lynwood stores, apartment buildings, and lots record footage that is overwritten within days. Getting a preservation demand out early, along with your own photos of the scene, can make or break a premises claim.

items.title: Deadlines and shared fault are manageable
items.desc: You generally have two years to file, but far less if a public entity is involved. California's pure comparative fault rule also means being partly at fault reduces a recovery rather than eliminating it, which an attorney can explain for your situation.

items.question: I fell on a sidewalk or at a city-owned building in Lynwood. Is the deadline different?
items.answer: Yes, and it is much shorter. When the property belongs to a public entity such as the City of Lynwood or Los Angeles County, you typically must file a formal government claim within about six months of the injury before any lawsuit can proceed. Missing that window can end the claim entirely, so speaking with an attorney soon after the fall matters.

items.question: The store manager said the spill had just happened. Does that end my case?
items.answer: Not by itself. The question is whether the business knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard, and a manager's statement is only one piece of that picture. Surveillance video, sweep logs, and employee schedules often tell a fuller story about how long the floor was wet and whether anyone checked it.

items.question: I was looking at my phone when I tripped. Can I still bring a claim?
items.answer: Possibly. California follows pure comparative fault, which means your own share of responsibility reduces what you can recover but does not automatically bar the claim. The property owner still had a duty to address hazards they knew or should have known about, and an attorney can weigh how those factors interact in your case.
